titleStmt.title: Combining Event-Triggered and Time-Triggered Traffic In FTT-CAN: Analysis of the Asynchronous Messaging System

analytic.title: Combining Event-Triggered and Time-Triggered Traffic In FTT-CAN: Analysis of the Asynchronous Messaging System

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: For some years there has been a debate opposing event-triggered and time-triggered trafic paradigms in jleldbuses. While the former is better suited to sporadic sources of information, the latter is more suited to periodic streams of information. However, for certain applications such as flexible real-time systems, a combination of both paradigms is desirable.

div.head: The authors have recently proposed a new CAN--based protocol that supports time-triggered communication in ajlexible way (FZ-CAN). It also allows an eficient combination of both time-triggered and eventtriggered trafic with temporal isolation. This paper describes the asynchronous messaging system of FTT-CAN which is responsible for the support of eventtriggered trafic. Furthermore, a response time analysis is carried out concerning the handling of asynchronous communication requests.
Introduction 1.Event vs Time-triggered communication
div.p: During several years, the fieldbus research community has known several debates which opposed different concepts and paradigms [ 11, e.g., static versus dynamic, synchronous versus asynchronous, deterministic versus non-deterministic, etc. One of such debates concerns the paradigm used for application architectures with event-triggered ones being opposed to those based on time-triggering [2]. One of the aspects of this debate is the discussion between the advantages and disadvantages of using either event-triggered or time-triggered communication. This discussion has been fostered by the appearance of the Time-Triggered Protocol -' M' P [3] that highlighted the advantages of that paradigm in realtime communication systems.

Event-triggered communication does seem more ergonomic and even more resource efficient. However, when worst-case situations are considered, that efficiency is not verified. Since events are asynchronous by nature, a typical worst-case assumption is that all events that must be handled by the system will arrive simultaneously. In order to cope with such situation in a timely fashion the required amount of resources (e.g. network bandwidth) is very high. On the contrary, the time-triggered approach forces the communication activity to occur at pre-defined instants in time at a rate determined by the dynamics of the environment under control. One of the features of this approach is that it allows relative phase control of the several streams of messages that must be transmitted over the communication system. By using this feature, messages of different streams can be set out-of-phase so that the number of messages that become ready for transmission simultaneously is substantially reduced. This feature is responsible for one of the most important properties of time-triggered communication as stressed by Kopetz [4], i.e. the support for composability with respect to the temporal behaviour. This property assures that, when two subsystems are integrated to form a new system, the temporal behaviour of each of them will not be affected. This does not hold true for event-triggered communication. In this case, the level of contention at the network access that each subsystem feels before integration is always increased upon integration due to the traffic generated by the other subsystem.

Furthermore, the relative phase control allowed by the time-triggered approach may lead to two other positive effects. Firstly, it improves the control over the transmission jitter felt by periodic message streams, an important aspect for control applications. Secondly, it supports higher network utilization with timeliness guarantees. Therefore, when considering worst-case situations the time-triggered approach is more resource efficient than the event-triggered one. However, when considering average-case situations, time-triggered communication is considerably more greedy than eventtriggered one. This latter aspect points out another compromise between the two paradigms. By dimensioning a system according to its worst-case requirements, as typical in hard real-time systems, the time-triggered approach tends to be less expensive than the event-triggered one due to its higher efficiency in such conditions. However, since the average network utilization of event-triggered systems is normally lower, such systems can easily support other sorts of communication with less stringent or no timing constraints (e.g. traffic associated with the management of either remote nodes or network) without any additional cost. This fact can have a positive impact on the overall efficiency of the communication system utilization, thus leading to reduce its exploitation costs.

div.head: Why combining both paradigms
div.p: Apart from the above considerations on network utilization, it is commonly accepted [1,5] that timetriggered communication is well adapted to control applications that typically require regular transmission of state data with low, or bounded, jitter (e.g. motion control, engine control, temperature control, position control). On the other hand, event-triggered communication is well adapted to the monitoring of alarm conditions that are supposed to occur sporadically and seldomly, and also to support asynchronous non-realtime traffic e.g. for global system management.

However, many applications do require simultaneous support for cyclic transmission of state data, sporadic transmission of alarms as well as of non-real-time data for system management. Hence, a combination of both paradigms in order to share their advantages seems desirable, particularly if it is possible to enforce a temporal isolation of both sorts of traffic. Otherwise, the event-triggered traffic would spoil the properties of the time-triggered one. With such combination it is then possible to use a time-triggered approach to manage the periodic real-time traffic with controlled jitter and with high efficiency under worst-case requirements. Simultaneously, a portion of the network bandwidth is kept available for sporadic event-triggered traffic, either realtime (e.g. alarms) as well as non-real-time (e.g. on-line management and reconfiguration). Flexible real-time systems in general, i.e. those that cope with dynamic requirements, are possible examples of systems that benefit from such a combination since they make use of all sorts of traffic referred before.

The importance of enforcing temporal isolation between the two sorts of traffic has already been referred above. A typical solution is to use the elementary cycle concept, i.e. a fixed duration window composed of two phases, one for each sort of traffic (e.g. discussed by Raja and Noubir [6]). The bus time is then slotted in elementary cycles resulting in an alternate sequence of time-triggered and event-triggered phases. The maximum duration of each phase can be tailored to suit the needs of a particular application. If each sort of traffic is forced to remain within the respective phase then, temporal isolation is guaranteed. This concept is used, for example, in the WorldFIP fieldbus [7]. However, since this fieldbus uses a MAC protocol based on centralised arbitration, the handling of event-triggered 68 (aperiodic) traffic is rather inefficient requiring a considerable amount of bandwidth to allow the master node (arbitrator) to become aware of aperiodic requests. In the Foundation Fieldbus [8], one of the 8 profiles of the new international fieldbus standard, a somewhat similar scheme is used. Instead of an elementary cycle, a particular node known as Link Active Scheduler contains the schedule for the time-triggered traffic. This node grants the other nodes, Link Masters, the permission to control the bus and transmit eventtriggered messages during precise time windows, only, that do not overlap with the time used by the timetriggered messages.

In many other fieldbus systems, that do not use the elementary cycle concept, it is still possible to specify cyclic time-triggered data exchanges but with no temporal isolation from the event-triggered traffic, e.g. PROFIBUS [7], CAL [9], DeviceNet [lo].

div.head: About this paper
div.p: This paper deals with a CAN-based protocol that supports flexible time-triggered communication, the FTT-CAN protocol [11,12]. Furthermore, both timetriggered and event-triggered traffic are supported, with temporal isolation being achieved by means of the double-phase elementary cycle concept. The former type of traffic is handled in the synchronous phase and the latter in the asynchronous one. The paper focuses on the FIT-CAN asynchronous messaging system which is briefly presented in section 2. The effective positioning of the two phases within the elementary cycle is analysed in section 3. Section 4 presents the response time analysis for asynchronous communication requests which might be of interest whenever the asynchronous messaging system is used to support real-time eventtriggered traffic. Section 5 concludes the paper.

div.head: FTT-CAN Asynchronous Messaging System
div.p: The FIT-CAN (Flexible Time-Triggered communication on CAN) protocol has been briefly presented in [ l l ] and further developed in [12]. A feature that distinguishes this protocol from other proposals concerning time-triggered communication on CAN [5] is that it supports dynamic communication requirements by using centralised scheduling with on-line admission control whilst the communication overhead is kept low by using the native distributed arbitration of CAN. Moreover, this distributed arbitration is also used to simplify the handling of asynchronous communication requests, resulting in reduced overhead and, consequently, in shorter response times.

In FTT-CAN a particular node, the master, generates a periodic message used to synchronize all other nodes in the network. The transmission of this message The FTT-CAN protocol also supports asynchronous traffic for event-triggered communication with external control. This sort of traffic is transmitted during the periods of the EC not used by the synchronous messages. However, depending on how the desired temporal isolation between these two sorts of traffic is enforced, the asynchronous messaging system (AMS) can operate in one of two modes. In controlled mode any asynchronous message is transmitted only if it is guaranteed not to interfere with the timeliness of the EC trigger message or of the synchronous messages. In this mode each station that produces asynchronous messages is allowed to transmit them only if there is enough bustime left within a specified time window, the asynchronous window. This enforces a strict temporal isolation between synchronous and asynchronous traffic. On the other hand, two negative aspects can be identified, the insertion of bus idle-time when asynchronous messages do not fit in the respective window and the need to force all the nodes in the system to follow the synchronisation imposed by the EC trigger message in order to determine the exact duration of each phase in each EC.
In uncontrolled mode, stations wishing to transmit asynchronous messages can try to do it as soon as they receive the respective requests from the application.

There is no need to synchronise with the EC trigger message and thus, even stations not engaged in the FIT-CAN protocol can coexist in the system and send asynchronous messages. Although these messages may now cause a certain blocking to the transmission of synchronous ones, such blocking can be upper bounded by using a proper choice of identifiers.

In FIT-CAN the message identifier range is divided in two parts. Higher priority identifiers are assigned to synchronous messages while lower priority identifiers are assigned to the asynchronous ones. In particular, the EC trigger message is assigned the highest priority identifier. Therefore, each group of consecutive synchronous messages, i.e., transmitted without releasing the bus arbitration process, can suffer blocking by, at most, one asynchronous message.

The advantages of this mode are twofold. Firstly, FIT-CAN can be installed in an existing system while keeping some of the legacy nodes not engaged' in the new protocol. Secondly, under uncontrolled mode there is no inserted idle-time as in controlled mode, thus allowing for higher bus utilization.

The price to pay is a bounded degradation of the synchronous and trigger message timings, i.e. increased jitter. How much is this degradation depends strongly on the particular bus controllers used. For example, when Full-CAN controllers (with multiple transmission buffers) are used, all the synchronous messages scheduled for one EC are transmitted without any intermediate blocking (at most one blocking in the beginning). On the other hand, if Basic-CAN controllers (with a single transmission buffer) are used, then, each time a node produces more than one synchronous message in the same EC there may be extra blockings. In this case, the controlled mode might be more appropriate. Tindel et al. [ 131 clearly show the difference between these two types of controllers in terms of realtime performance.
In this paper, either the use of Full-CAN controllers, or Basic-CAN but with each node producing at most one synchronous message, will be considered.

div.head: Arranging syndasync phases in the EC
div.p: When implementing the FIT-CAN protocol, it is important to define how the synchronous and asynchronous phases will be combined within the EC. In preliminar experimental work, two different options have been considered: the synchronous phase starting right after the EC trigger message and starting after a fixed period of time called scanning window [ 1 I]. In this section, these options, plus a third one considering that synchronous messages are always transmitted at the end of the EC, are analysed and compared. These three situations are referred to as: synchronous phase scheduled as soon as possible, scheduled after a fixed period of time (scanning window), and scheduled as late as possible.

div.head: Sync phase scheduled as soon as possible
div.p: In this situation, the synchronous messages are produced as soon as they are identified by the producers, i.e. in the beginning of the EC, right after the trigger message (fig. 2-a). Notice, however, that before starting the transmission of any synchronous message all nodes require a certain time to scan their local tables and identify themselves as producers in that EC (appears as p in fig. 2-a). This time can be small (relative to the transmission time of one message) when using powerful microprocessors, or it can be larger when low processing-power microcontrollers are used'. In any case, all nodes engaged in the protocol release the bus during this period of time p. If there were asynchronous messages pending, at least one of them could gain access to the bus and eventually delay the start of transmission of the synchronous messages. Moreover, the amount of time p varies with the relative position of each synchronous message in the local table. Hence, to enforce a strict temporal isolation between both types of traffic, as desired in the asynchronous controlled mode, asynchronous messages are released for transmission only after the synchronous phase is over. Notice that, in this case, the amount of bus-time p is wasted, a situation that is particularly negative when using low processingpower microcontrollers. Furthermore, to strictly maintain the regularity of the EC trigger message, a variable amount of idle-time a, upper bounded by the time to transmit one message, is inserted at the end of the asynchronous phase.

div.head: Sync phase scheduled after fixed period of time
div.p: In an attempt to make the time spent in scanning the local table (p) usable by asynchronous traffic even under controlled mode, a scanning window of fixed duration was defined between the end of the trigger message and the start of the synchronous phase (fig. 2-b). The asynchronous phase is now divided in two parts, one corresponding to the scanning window and another one corresponding to the time left after the synchronous phase. In any of these parts, under controlled mode, messages are transmitted only if they can be guaranteed to fit in the respective windows. Otherwise, they are delayed to the following ECs. This corresponds to the insertion of idle-time (a), in each part, to enforce the regularity of the trigger and synchronous messages.

div.head: Sync phase scheduled as late as possible
div.p: This option, also referred to as dynamic scanning window, has the major advantage over the previous ones of maximising the time available to asynchronous messages within one EC and keeping it all together (fig. timeliness of the synchronous messages is required at most once per EC, leading to a higher average capacity to handle asynchronous messages. This arrangement of the two phases can easily be accomplished by also using the EC trigger message to convey the duration of the asynchronous phase, e.g. using low order bits of the message identifier. This can be carried out with minimal extra run-time overhead. Another interesting feature is that when a message transmission request is aborted because it does not fit in the current asynchronous window, it is delayed until the next EC. However, the request is resubmitted during the transmission of the trigger message of the next EC so that it re-enters arbitration in the very beginning of the next asynchronous window. This detail assures that there will be no further priority inversions whenever an asynchronous message is delayed from EC to EC until it is transmitted.

Furthermore, since the most regular edge of the synchronous phase, in terms of periodicity, is now the ending edge (near the next EC trigger message), the higher priority synchronous messages must be transmitted later within the respective phase in order to reduce jitter. This is achieved by assigning lower priority identifiers to higher priority synchronous messages (notice that the priority of the synchronous messages and the respective identifiers are different parameters [ 1 13).

div.head: Choosing an arrangement
div.p: The three situations referred above were analysed concerning, particularly, their use under the asynchronous controlled mode. In such mode, scheduling the synchronous phase as late as possible seems to be more advantageous leading to a more efficient bus utilization. This is particularly true when using low processingpower microcontrollers.

With uncontrolled mode the differences between those three situations are not so evident. In fact, in this case possible blockings caused by asynchronous messages are inevitable in any situation. Such blockings may occur if an asynchronous message is still being transmitted when the EC trigger message is released or when the synchronous window starts. However, as it will be seen in section 4, the response time analysis will also be easier to carry out, and more precise, when the block of synchronous and trigger messages is transmitted in a row, i.e. without pre-emption. This is achieved, only, when the synchronous phase is scheduled as late as possible.
Therefore, only this arrangement will be considered in the remainder of the paper with the asynchronous phase first, followed by the synchronous one.

div.head: Worst-case response time of asynchronous messages
div.p: It has already been said that the asynchronous messaging system in FIT-CAN is meant to support event-triggered traffic either real-time (e.g. alarms) as well as non-real-time (e.g. management data). For the former one, the response time of the communication system to each request, particularly under worst-case conditions, is an important parameter. Therefore, this section is devoted to the analysis of such worst-case response time defined as the time lapse that mediates between a transmission request, at the datalink level, and the actual complete message transmission. Message queuing at the transmitter (so as de-queuing at the receiver) is not considered in this analysis.

div.head: Scheduling of synchronous traffic
div.p: Since the protocol gives higher priority to the synchronous traffic, any timing analysis requires a clear understanding of the mechanisms used by the synchronous messaging system (SMS). This system is mainly controlled by a particular node called Distributor, or Master, which holds several centralised data structures used for scheduling. The most important of these is the Synchronous Requirements Table (SRT), where each entry describes one message stream. The SRT is organised as follows: SRT = { SM, (DLC, Ci Phi Pi Di Pri), i=l .. N, ) DLC is data length in bytes (from 0 to 8), C is the respective maximum transmission time (including stuff bits), Ph stands for the relative phasing, P for period, D for deadline and Pr for fixed priority. Both Ph and P are expressed as integer multiples of the EC duration (E). The CAN identifier of each message is formed by adding the index i to a given offset. Normally, there will be an appropriate relationship between identifier and the priority Pr. Ns is the number of synchronous messages.

Based on the SRT, a planning scheduler builds a Schedule Table (SchT) that describes the synchronous traffic for a fixed period of time into the future called a plan [14]. This table is organised as a finite sequence of ECs and, for each EC, it contains the identification of which synchronous messages shall be produced. Notice that the SchT is not necessarily cyclic and so the scheduler is constantly rebuilding the next SchT for successive plans. Changes from one plan to the next are smooth, that is, at the beginning of a plan the initial phases for each message stream are updated according to their last instance in the previous plan. Thus, the periodicity of the synchronous messages is respected (not counting with delays cuased by mutual interference).

Each column is transmitted at the start of each EC in the data field of the respective EC trigger message. Notice that the trigger message transaction has a duration defined at set-up time (LTM), which depends on the maximum number of synchronous messages.

div.head: Analysis of the asynchronous uncontrolled mode
div.p: As explained before, under uncontrolled mode, requests to transmit asynchronous messages can be made at any time. The nodes connected to the network do not need to be aware of the synchronous messaging system. However, there is one basic constraint that must be followed in order to bound the interference that these messages can cause to the timeliness of the synchronous system. The CAN identifiers used by asynchronous messages must always be of lower priority than those used by the synchronous or trigger messages. An easy way to accomplish this separation is to assign half of the identifier range to each class. This way only one bit is required to determine which is the type of a message.

The interference referred above can reveal itself both as a jitter of the EC trigger message or as an additional jitter of the synchronous messages (fig. 6) beyond any existent jitter inherent to the synchronous scheduling strategy used and to other factors such as variation in number of stuff bits.

Concerning the maximum trigger message jitter (JTM), it appears as a consequence of variations on the start of the previous synchronous phase which can be delayed by an asynchronous message that gained access to the bus before. In the worst-case JTM can equal the maximum delay that happens when the last synchronous message that began transmission just before the release of the trigger message, is the longest of all synchronous messages (duration Cs). However, when there are no messages within the synchronous phase of a given EC, the trigger message may suffer a delay equal to the duration of the longest asynchronous message (Ca) which could have been released just before. Thus, an upper bound to the jitter that can be induced to the trigger message by asynchronous ones is given by (7). JTM = max( Cs, Ca) (7) On the other hand, the maximum additional jitter induced on the synchronous messages (JSM) by the asynchronous ones results from the cumulative contribution of two factors: the blocking caused by an asynchronous message to the whole synchronous phase and the trigger message jitter. The influence of this latter factor is due to the start of the synchronous window being referenced to the end of the trigger message. A bound to such additional jitter (JSM) can be obtained by maximising both factors (fig. 6).

When the latest synchronous messages scheduled for a given EC suffer a delay equal to JSM, they can be carried on to the following EC, being transmitted after the next trigger message which uses a higher priority identifier. This fact increases their delay by the duration of the trigger message LTM. Hence, the upper bound JSM can be obtained from (8). Moreover, it is small compared to the EC duration which is typically set to hold the transmission of several (>lo) longest messages (8 data bytes).

In fact, the only difference is the non-existence of inserted idle-time. This allows for a higher bus utilization and lower response times. One operational detail that must be enforced is that the request for the transmission of the trigger message must be issued before the end of transmission of the last synchronous message. div.head: A word on errors in CAN
div.p: The analysis presented in the previous sections did not consider transmission errors. In fact, due to their stochastic nature, deterministic approaches to response time analysis cannot be used to cope with them. Probabilistic approaches should, then, be used (e.g. [15]).

One of the main problems with errors in CAN is the automatic retransmission upon error detection embodied in the protocol. This automatic retransmission spoils any temporal framework for the transmission of messages which means that it is incompatible with a time-triggered approach. For this reason, there is a current trend to introduce in IS0 11898 CAN standard the possibility to disable the automatic retransmission [ 161. Furthermore, some recent CAN controllers already include this feature known as single shot transmission.

There is on-going work concerning the analysis of the effect that errors on FTT-CAN. When standard CAN controllers are used, i.e. with the current standard error handling features, there should be some care in order to avoid very high bus utilization factors (not quantified yet). The remaining bus capacity is necessary to accommodate the transmission of error flags and retransmissions that may eventually occur.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This paper discusses the advantages and disadvantages of event and time triggered paradigms in fieldbus communication systems. It also stresses the advantages that may arise from a combination of both paradigms but in a way that enforces temporal isolation between the two types of traffic. This allows to maintain the respective temporal properties resulting in two different communication subsystems co-existing in the same physical system.

Then, it is shown how such combination can be achieved with FTT-CAN protocol which was designed primarily to support time-triggered communication on CAN in a flexible way. This combination results in the co-existence of two subsystems, the synchronous messaging system (SMS) and the asynchronous messaging system (AMs), for time and event-triggered traffic, respectively. The actual implementation of AMS together with SMS under FTT-CAN is discussed in detail. Two operating modes for AMS are presented, namely controlled and uncontrolled. While the former one enforces a strict temporal isolation between the two types of traffic, the latter allows for a bounded interference. On the other hand, uncontrolled mode allows for a higher degree of flexibility, being possible to join in the same system nodes engaged and not engaged in the protocol as long as the messages transmitted by the latter ones use lower priority identifiers. The paper ends with an analysis of the response time to asynchronous communication requests. This analysis is of particular interest when asynchronous messages are used to convey real-time data, e.g. alarms.
